source_text: Φθάσαντες δ᾿ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω εἰρήκαμεν περὶ τοῦ τὸν Χριστὸν προφητεύεσθαι δύο ἐπιδημίαις χρησόμενον εἰς τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένος· διόπερ οὐκέτι χρεία ἡμᾶς ἀπολογήσασθαι πρὸς τὸ λεγόμενον ὡς ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἰουδαίου, ὅτι μέγαν καὶ δυνάστην καὶ πάσης τῆς γῆς καὶ πάντων τῶν ἐθνῶν καὶ στρατοπέδων κύριόν φασιν οἱ προφῆται εἶναι τὸν ἐπιδημήσοντα. Ἰουδαϊκῶς δ᾿ οἶμαι εἶπε καὶ κατὰ τὴν ἐκείνων χολὴν μετὰ τοῦ χωρὶς ἀποδείξεως κἂν πιθανῶς λοιδορεῖν τὸν Ἰησοῦν. ὅτι οὐχὶ (δὲ) τοιοῦτον ὄλεθρον κατήγγειλαν. καίτοι οὔτε Ἰουδαῖοι οὔτε Κέλσος οὔτε ἄλλος τις μετὰ ἀποδείξεως ἔχει παραστῆσαι ὅτι ὄλεθρος τοσούτους ἀνθρώπους ἐπιστρέφει ἀπὸ τῆς χύσεως τῶν κακῶν ἐπὶ τὸν κατὰ φύσιν μετὰ σωφροσύνης καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ἀρετῶν βίον.
pass_a_gloss: Having anticipated (φθάσαντες), we have said in the things above about Christ being prophesied as going to make use of two comings/sojourns (ἐπιδημίαι) to the race of humans; therefore there is no longer need for us to make defence (ἀπολογήσασθαι) against what is said as by the Jew, that the prophets say the one who will come (ἐπιδημήσοντα) is great (μέγας) and a mighty ruler (δυνάστης) and lord (κύριος) of all the earth and of all the nations and armies (στρατόπεδα). But in Jewish fashion (Ἰουδαϊκῶς), I think, he spoke, and according to their gall/bitterness (χολή), together with reviling (λοιδορεῖν) Jesus without proof (ἀπόδειξις), even plausibly (κἂν πιθανῶς): that they did not announce (κατήγγειλαν) such a pest/destruction (ὄλεθρος). And yet neither Jews nor Celsus nor anyone else can establish with proof that a pest turns (ἐπιστρέφει) so many people from the outpouring/flood (χύσις) of evils to the life according to nature (κατὰ φύσιν) with self-control (σωφροσύνη) and the remaining virtues (ἀρεταί).
pass_b_english: We have already spoken earlier about Christ’s being foretold as one who would make two comings to the human race. So we no longer need to answer what is said, as if by the Jew, that the prophets declare the one who is to come to be great, a mighty ruler, and lord of all the earth and of all the nations and armies.

But it was in Jewish fashion, I think, and out of their bitterness, that he said, while reviling Jesus without proof, not even a plausible one, that the prophets did not proclaim such a plague. Yet neither the Jews nor Celsus nor anyone else can show with proof that a plague turns so many people from a flood of evils to the life that accords with nature, with self-control and the other virtues.

translator_notes: ‘We have already spoken earlier’ refers to Origen’s treatment of the two comings of Christ in Book 1 (around 1.56). The Jew’s claim about what the prophets say, and his claim that they did not proclaim ‘such a pest’, are reported in indirect speech (ὅτι clauses), so no quotation marks; ‘as if by the Jew’ keeps Origen’s framing. ‘ὄλεθρος’ used of a person = a plague, a ruinous creature; rendered ‘plague’ in both places (reviewer: ‘pest’ read as a mere nuisance in modern English) to keep Origen’s retort on the same word. ‘χωρὶς ἀποδείξεως κἂν πιθανῶς’ is compressed: either ‘without proof, not even a plausible one’ (adopted) or ‘without proof, though perhaps plausibly’. The ’(δὲ)’ bracketed in the edition is an editorial supplement and adds nothing to the English. No specific Scripture text quoted; the description of the coming ruler is Celsus’s summary of prophetic hopes, not a single verse.
